politician.name: Ed Markey
politician.bio: Ed Markey is a Democrat who has served as a U.S. Senator from Massachusetts since 2013, when he won a special election to fill the seat vacated by John Kerry. In 2026 he is seeking re-election against Republican John Deaton after defeating Rep. Seth Moulton in the Sept. 1 Democratic primary. He previously represented Massachusetts in the U.S. House from 1976 to 2013 and served in the Massachusetts House of Representatives from 1973 to 1976.

career_history.role: U.S. Representative from Massachusetts (7th district; 5th district in 2013)

summary:
Sen. Ed Markey and Republican John Deaton met Oct. 13 at WBZ-TV in what outlets described as their only scheduled debate before the Nov. 3 election [1][2]. Markey repeatedly sought to tie Deaton to President Trump, saying his opponent would be "a blank check for Donald Trump" and arguing that a Deaton win would help preserve the Republican Senate majority [1][3]. Markey invoked Trump more than 40 times over the hour-long debate, according to Boston.com, and called Deaton's effort to be both an independent and a Republican an oxymoron [1][2]. Deaton countered that he has never voted for, supported, or endorsed Trump, and accused Markey of misrepresenting his record and being part of a hyper-partisan Washington [1][3].

On policy, Markey pressed for Medicare for All, cited Medicaid cuts in the Republican-passed One Big Beautiful Bill Act, and defended the Green New Deal while criticizing the Trump administration for halting offshore wind projects [2][3]. Deaton argued that Markey has been unable to win over most Senate Democrats on Medicare for All, proposed breaking up large insurance companies instead, and said Markey's energy agenda relies on costly mandates, favoring nuclear power and natural gas [1][3]. Deaton also questioned whether the 80-year-old senator could be effective over another six-year term and raised Markey's 2002 vote to authorize the Iraq War, which Markey has called a mistake, while Markey dismissed such attacks as red herrings [1][2]. Both candidates voiced support for safeguards on artificial intelligence, and Markey declined Deaton's on-stage request for a second debate in western Massachusetts [2].

Polling reported during the period showed Markey with a wide lead: a MassINC poll cited by MassLive had him ahead 54% to 28%, a UMass Amherst/WCVB survey taken Oct. 5 to 12 showed him leading 56% to 29%, and a Suffolk University/Boston Globe poll put his support at about 60%, with nearly 45% of respondents saying they had never heard of Deaton [4][5][6]. FEC filings through Oct. 14 show Markey with about $800,000 cash on hand and Deaton with about $488,000, after Deaton loaned his own campaign $1 million [4][9].

In the Senate, Markey and Sen. Jeff Merkley introduced a joint resolution of disapproval on Oct. 15 seeking to block the Trump administration's civilian nuclear agreement with Saudi Arabia over concerns that it lacks adequate guardrails against weapons development, though The Hill reported the measure faces long odds because reversing the deal would require Trump's signature [7]. Markey also joined other members of the Massachusetts congressional delegation in asking the Department of Homeland Security's inspector general to investigate conditions at ICE's Burlington field office, while a DHS spokesperson said the facility complies with state and local laws and called claims of inadequate conditions false [8].
